definition: A third-party beneficiary is a person or entity that is not a party to a contract but may enforce a promise in the contract because the contracting parties intended to confer an enforceable benefit on that person or entity. The party who makes the promise is the promisor, and the party to whom the promise is made is the promisee. Generally, a nonparty cannot sue for breach of contract, but the third-party-beneficiary doctrine creates an exception. Courts distinguish an intended beneficiary from an incidental beneficiary. An intended beneficiary is a third party whom the contracting parties planned to benefit in a way that the particular jurisdiction treats as enforceable. An incidental beneficiary may receive a benefit from the performance of a contract, but cannot enforce the contract because conferring an enforceable right was not an objective of the agreement. Merely receiving some advantage from a contract is generally not enough to establish third-party-beneficiary rights. The distinction depends heavily on the language and purpose of the particular contract. A classic example is Lawrence v. Fox, 20 N.Y. 268 (1859). In this case, Holly owed Lawrence $300. Holly then loaned Fox $300 after Fox promised Holly that he would pay that amount to Lawrence. When Fox failed to pay, the New York Court of Appeals allowed Lawrence to enforce the promise even though Lawrence was not a party to the agreement between Holly and Fox. Because contract law is primarily state law, the precise test for third-party-beneficiary status varies by jurisdiction. California Civil Code § 1559, for example, provides that a contract made expressly for the benefit of a third person may be enforced by that person before the contracting parties rescind it. In Goonewardene v. ADP, LLC, 6 Cal. 5th 817 (2019), the California Supreme Court explained that a third party must show that they would in fact benefit from the contract, that providing the benefit was a motivating purpose of the contracting parties, and that allowing enforcement would be consistent with the contract's objectives and the contracting parties' reasonable expectations. New York applies its own test.
